title: Specifying Research Cluster 2
text:
Research Community Word Clouds
One method of exploring the substantive content of the smaller research communities within each of the 8 Research Clusters is through a word cloud. Below, keywords are sized and coloured by PageRank calculated within each community (included in parentheses after each keyword)1. This means PageRank measures how structurally central a keyword is to a particular community, taking into account both its connections to other keywords in the community and the centrality of those connected terms. The largest and darkest words can be read as the community’s organizing vocabulary.. For convenience, the colour of the word clouds corresponds to the colour of the community found in Research Cluster 2 Keyword Network (above). For the sake of clarity, only the 50 most central keywords from each community are captured in the word clouds. In some cases, research communities contained fewer than 50 keywords.

Research Community 1

This community can reasonably be characterized as focusing on gender, social identity, discrimination, and social difference, with an emphasis on how these processes operate in institutional and cultural contexts. The most structurally central terms include gender (0.009), women (0.009), Canada (0.008), United States (0.007), attitudes (0.006), discrimination (0.006), identity (0.005), men (0.005), culture (0.005), and gender-differences (0.005). Together, these terms indicate a literature organized around gendered and other forms of social differentiation, their relationship to identity, and the attitudes and discriminatory processes associated with them.





Keyword Terms: Community 1, Research Cluster 2




A second strand concerns the institutional and social settings in which these differences are experienced. Education (0.005), power (0.005), stigma (0.005), participation (0.004), race (0.004), religion (0.004), employment (0.003), immigration (0.003), and language (0.003) suggest research on how identity and social difference are shaped through institutions, cultural contexts, and patterns of inclusion and exclusion. The prominence of Canada and United States also indicates that geographic context is an important feature of the community.
The community also contains a substantial sexuality-related component. Sex (0.004), sexual orientation (0.003), gay men (0.003), attractiveness (0.003), fertility (0.002), and intersectionality (0.003) extend the focus beyond gender alone toward sexuality and overlapping forms of social identity.
Proposed title: Gender, social identity, discrimination, and inequality

Research Community 2

The PageRank structure suggests that this community is primarily organized around research on personnel assessment and selection, particularly the processes through which organizations evaluate job applicants and the ways applicants respond to those processes. The strongest evidence comes from the most structurally central terms: behavior (.048), selection (.047), personality (.047), perceptions (.044), model (.043), and validity (.0390). These are joined by a more specific set of highly central terms—impression management (.039), employment interview (.037), ratings (.035), faking (.034), applicant reactions (.034), and self-presentation (.032)—that locate the cluster more specifically within the study of employee selection, interviewing, and applicant behaviour.





Keyword Terms: Community 2, Research Cluster 2




A second group of terms indicates that the community is concerned not simply with selection procedures themselves, but with their measurement properties and consequences. Job-performance, reliability, personnel-selection, ability, individual-differences, organizational justice, accuracy, decisions, bias, and tests point toward questions about whether selection methods predict performance, measure applicants reliably, and produce fair or accurate judgments. Meanwhile, technology, asynchronous video interviews, social media, and artificial intelligence suggest a strand concerned with technologically mediated or newer forms of recruitment and assessment.
Proposed title: personnel selection, assessment, and employment interviewing

Research Community 3

This community is best characterized as a research area concerned with corporate governance, financial reporting, and firm performance. The most structurally central terms include impact (0.007), performance (0.007), information (0.005), quality (0.005), market (0.005), and corporate governance (0.005). Together with earnings (0.004), firm performance (0.004), firms (0.004), and firm (0.004), these terms indicate a literature organized around explaining corporate outcomes and the informational and governance conditions associated with them.





Keyword Terms: Community 3, Research Cluster 2




A second strand concerns financial reporting and governance mechanisms. Earnings (0.004), disclosure (0.004), earnings management (0.004), agency costs (0.004), ownership (0.004), and compensation (0.004) point to research on the production and quality of corporate information, managerial incentives, and the structures through which firms are governed. These terms suggest recurring attention to how reporting practices and governance arrangements shape firm behaviour and performance.
The community also has a clear corporate finance and market dimension. Risk (0.004), investment (0.003), returns (0.003), and equity (0.003) connect governance and disclosure questions to financial-market outcomes. China (0.003), environment (0.003), and corporate social-responsibility (0.003) appear as important contextual or secondary strands.
Proposed title: Corporate governance, financial reporting, and firm performance

Research Community 4

This community can be characterized as being focused on environmental governance, sustainability, and climate adaptation. The most structurally central terms—management (0.011), governance (0.007), sustainability (0.007), adaptation (0.007), framework (0.007), policy (0.006), systems (0.006), and knowledge (0.006)—indicate a literature concerned with how environmental problems are organized, governed, and managed.





Keyword Terms: Community 4, Research Cluster 2




The community also has a clear institutional and implementation-oriented dimension. Organizations (0.005), politics (0.005), implementation (0.005), comanagement (0.004), and agency (0.004) suggest attention to the actors, institutions, and arrangements through which environmental policies and strategies are carried out. At the same time, science (0.005), uncertainty (0.005), scale (0.005), resilience (0.005), and systems (0.006) indicate a systems-oriented literature concerned with complexity, knowledge, and decision-making under changing environmental conditions.
A secondary strand connects these environmental and governance questions to human populations and livelihoods. Migration (0.005), poverty (0.005), livelihoods (0.004), Bangladesh (0.004), and fisheries (0.004) suggest attention to the social consequences of environmental change and resource governance, particularly in contexts of vulnerability.
Proposed title: Environmental governance, sustainability, and climate adaptation

Research Community 5

This community is best characterized as workplace health, well-being, and organizational behaviour. The most structurally central terms—work (0.008), health (0.007), stress (0.007), workplace (0.006), mental health (0.006), support (0.006), and well-being (0.005)—point to research concerned with the relationship between working conditions and employee psychological and health outcomes. Burnout (0.005) and depression (0.005) further indicate a focus on adverse consequences of work and workplace experiences.





Keyword Terms: Community 5, Research Cluster 2




A second strand concerns leadership and organizational relationships. Transformational leadership (0.006), leadership (0.005), satisfaction (0.005), commitment (0.005), social support (0.005), resources (0.005), and trust (0.004) suggest research examining how leadership, organizational resources, and interpersonal support relate to employee attitudes and well-being. The presence of incivility (0.005) and abusive supervision (0.004) provides the corresponding negative side of these workplace relationships, linking supervisory and interpersonal conditions to employee outcomes.
The community also has an applied dimension. Intervention (0.005), training (0.004), and prevention (0.004) indicate research concerned with improving workplace conditions and mitigating harmful outcomes.
Proposed title: Workplace health, well-being, and organizational behaviour

title: Research Cluster 1
text:
“Evolution” serves as reasonable umbrella for much of the material in Research Cluster 1 because its communities draw attention to how the things they study came to be and how they changed over time. Across these communities, a major through line is the use of evidence available today to reconstruct a history.
Questions of galaxy formation capture the first community. Its keywords trace how clouds of gas collapse, how young stars gather material from surrounding disks, and how stellar oscillations help researchers probe the structure of stars as they evolve. A secondary thread in this community focuses on evolution via sexual selection and population formation.
Geological considerations account for six of the nine keyword communities. Across these communities, researchers use rocks, minerals, and sediments to reconstruct how geological systems formed and changed. In Atlantic Canada, that work spans the assembly of the northern Appalachians and the history of offshore basins, where sandstones preserve evidence of where sediments came from and what happened after burial. Work in southern Mexico uses rock ages and deformation to reconstruct ancient plate boundaries, while research in northwest China examines both continental growth and basin development. The volcanic-rock geochemistry community follows the origins of magmas across tectonic settings, and the British Columbia community brings that interest in magmatic processes to questions about ore formation.
One keyword network points to questions about biological lineages and how they are classified, with a focus on grasses such as wheat, barley, and Elymus. Researchers compare DNA sequences and plant traits to trace ancestry and examine how interbreeding and changes in chromosome number have shaped relationships among lineages. Arabidopsis’ role as a plant model adds further support in suggesting that this community hinges on questions about plant biology more generally.
A separate community examines discrimination and the economic and social lives of sexual and gender minorities. Its keywords point to research on earnings and self-employment among gay men, lesbians, and same-sex couples, alongside questions about gender identity, inclusion, and mental health. Its presence in the cluster captures a distinct line of research on how people are treated and how they fare in markets and other social settings.
Below are two forms of information that together help characterize what the smaller keyword communities within this research cluster are “about.” The first is a word cloud in which each keyword’s font size reflects its within-community PageRank. PageRank measures a keyword’s structural prominence by considering both the strength of its connections and the prominence of the keywords connected to it. Because these scores depend on one another, the calculation accounts for connections across the entire community. Keywords shown in larger font therefore have greater structural prominence within that community. The second is a list of publications strongly affiliated with the community. Together, the word cloud and the affiliated publications offer a window into the research activity represented by the keyword network.

















I read this community as centred on how stars form and change over time. “Evolution” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.145), and the terms that follow it give the community an astrophysical focus. Hydrodynamic models, interstellar clouds, collapse, and accretion trace the formation of stars from clouds of gas and dust, while protostars and protoplanetary disks point to the early stages of stellar and planetary development. Research on stellar oscillations and metallicity extends that focus to the structure and evolution of stars.
I also see a strand of research in which evolution takes on a biological meaning, with a focus on sexual selection and population structure. Kinship, pairwise relatedness, and gene flow point to questions about how populations are structured. Research on sexual selection includes how body size and sexual size dimorphism relate to mating success, as well as how traits such as physical attractiveness and social cues such as reputation figure in mate preferences.

I read this community as research that uses the chemistry of rocks to reconstruct where magmas came from and how they changed before eruption. “Geochemistry” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.068), followed by “volcanic-rocks” and “petrogenesis,” the study of how rocks form. Trace elements and neodymium and strontium isotopes provide clues to the sources of magmas and to processes such as crystallization, mixing, and interaction with the continental crust. The tectonic terms give these questions a setting, from subduction and island arcs to continental rifting and volcanism associated with mantle plumes. Studies from the Canadian Cordillera, the Aegean, and the Himalaya–Tibet region show how this line of inquiry plays out across different geological settings.

I read this community as giving the cluster’s geological research a Maritime and northern Appalachian focus. Nova Scotia has the highest within-community PageRank (0.081), followed by New Brunswick, the Maritimes Basin, and the northern Appalachians. Where the geochemistry community studies how volcanic rocks form across a range of tectonic settings, this community uses geochemistry, uranium–lead dating, and petrology to reconstruct the history of a particular region. Studies of the South Mountain Batholith and the Cobequid Highlands bring that history into view at the scale of individual rock bodies and field areas, while work on sedimentary basins and terrane boundaries traces how the region took shape.

I read this community as a focus on the molecular evolution and classification of plant life, centred on grasses. “Origin” (0.055) and “classification” (0.052) have the highest within-community PageRank, followed by “Triticeae” and “Poaceae.” “Origin” in this context is most reasonably understood as “evolutionary ancestry”. The prominence of wheat, Hordeum, and Elymus gives the research a focus within the grass family. Arabidopsis, as a model plant used in biology, supports the suggestion that this community centres on plant biology. Keywords such as “RPB2 gene,” “chloroplast genome,” and “morphology” point to the evidence researchers use to reconstruct ancestry. Introgression, polyploidy, and multiple origins point to why those histories can be difficult to classify. This community develops a biological strand of the earlier evolution community by bringing questions of lineage and classification to the foreground. Alongside the geochemistry and Maritime geology communities, it adds another kind of historical reconstruction to the cluster, using genes and plant traits to trace how lineages formed.

I read this community as extending the cluster’s Maritime geological focus offshore, with an emphasis on where sediments came from and what happened to them after deposition. “Provenance” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.050), and the prominence of “offshore Nova Scotia,” “margin,” “sandstones,” and “basin” places that question on the eastern Canadian continental margin, particularly in the Scotian Basin. Stratigraphy and depositional facies point to how sediments accumulated, while diagenesis and thermal history point to how burial, heating, and fluid movement altered the resulting rocks. The closest overlap is with the Maritime and northern Appalachian community, which also studies basin development alongside granite emplacement and terrane assembly. The contrast with the geochemistry community is in what “origin” means: there the question is how magmas formed, while here it is where sediment grains came from and what they can tell us about the history of a basin.

This community adds a focus on discrimination and economic life to the cluster. “Discrimination” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.182), followed by “gay men,” “sexual orientation,” and “lesbians.” The prominence of “same-sex,” “couples,” “self-employment,” and “earnings” gives that focus a labour-market dimension, with questions about how individuals and couples make a living and how their economic outcomes differ. “Gender identity,” “inclusion,” and “mental health” extend the discussion to how people are treated and how they fare beyond earnings. The earlier evolution community also included research on sex differences and mate preferences. Here, sexuality figures in a different set of questions, about how social institutions and markets shape the lives of sexual and gender minorities.

This community adds a focus on how the rocks of southern Mexico record the movement of continents and the history of ancient oceans. “Geochronology” (0.063) has the highest within-community PageRank, followed by “Acatlán Complex” (0.061) and “Mexico” (0.055). The Acatlán and Oaxacan complexes give the research a regional anchor, while “Laurentia,” “Gondwana,” “Rheic Ocean,” and “Pangea” point to questions about where these blocks of crust once lay and how they came together. Dating establishes the sequence of events, while deformation and high-pressure metamorphism provide clues to how rocks were buried, transformed, and brought back toward the surface. The closest parallel is the Maritime and northern Appalachian community, which also uses rock ages and terrane relationships to reconstruct tectonic history. Here, the emphasis is on using a regional rock record to work out the former positions of continents and the oceans between them.

This community gives the cluster’s geological research a focus on continental growth and basin development in northwest China. “West Junggar” has the highest within-community PageRank (0.081), followed by “Sr–Nd” (0.073) and “continental growth” (0.070). Strontium and neodymium isotopes connect this community to the earlier work on volcanic-rock geochemistry. Here, “orogenic belt,” “remnant ocean basin,” and “ophiolitic mélange” place that evidence in the context of how continental crust grew as ocean basins closed. That question parallels the reconstruction of ancient plate boundaries in the southern Mexico community. The keywords also point to work on the Junggar Basin itself, where “Mahu Sag,” “rift basin,” “Fengcheng Formation,” and “provenance analysis” bring basin development, sediment sources, and past environments into view. This strand bears some resonance with Scotian Basin (check this) community, where sedimentary rocks also provide a record of how a basin developed.

This community brings ore formation to the foreground of the cluster’s geological research, with British Columbia as its named setting. All eight keywords have the same within-community PageRank , so the focus comes from reading them together. “Gold deposit,” “porphyry,” and “platinum-group elements” identify the kinds of deposits and metals under study, while “magmatic-hydrothermal fluids” and “ore genesis” point to questions about how fluids associated with magmas transport and concentrate metals. This overlaps with the volcanic-rock geochemistry community’s interest in magmatic processes and with the Maritime community’s work on mineralization, including the Kemptville tin deposit. Here, the question of how an ore deposit forms is the focus of the community.

title: Describing the SMU-affiliated Research Corpus
text:
The expansion of corporate management models within higher education over the past several decades has begun to change how academic knowledge is produced, evaluated, and incentivised. To greater and lesser degrees, universities have transitioned away from traditional collegial governance structures toward managerial frameworks, commonly known as New Public Management (NPM). Under this corporate paradigm, senior university administration relies on institutional strategic research plans, formal performance indicators, and centralised accountability metrics to align faculty behaviours with broader organisational objectives.
Below, I review some recent scholarship on academic managerialism to contextualise what for me, is becoming an increasinly intersting question: do strategic research plans work?

title: Describing the SMU-affiliated Research Corpus
text:
The expansion of corporate management models within higher education over the past several decades has begun to change how academic knowledge is produced, evaluated, and incentivised. To greater and lesser degrees, universities have transitioned away from traditional collegial governance structures toward managerial frameworks, commonly known as New Public Management (NPM). Under this corporate paradigm, senior university administration relies on institutional strategic research plans, formal performance indicators, and centralised accountability metrics to align faculty behaviours with broader organisational objectives.
Below, I review some recent scholarship on academic managerialism to contextualise what for me, is becoming an increasinly intersting question: do strategic research plans work?

title: Describing the SMU-affiliated Research Corpus
text:
Academic Managerialism
The introduction of corporate steering in public research sectors is frequently framed as a necessary mechanism to increase operational efficiency and institutional accountability. Scholars examining the Central and Eastern European contexts demonstrate that department heads are forced to act as primary mediators, negotiating the friction between emerging corporate managerial expectations and traditional academic autonomy (Machovcova, Zabrodska, and Mudrak 2019). This transition shifts the university from an open site of unconstrained intellectual inquiry to a managed environment where output is being both quantified and regularised. Empirical observations of these policy shifts suggest that while they aim to stimulate public research efficiency, they can function as a double-edged sword, leading to administrative inflation and narrow publishing strategies among faculty (Schubert 2009).
The global reach of these corporate practices is evident across diverse higher education landscapes, including developing regions such as the United Arab Emirates, where new managerialism is deployed to reshape institutional reputations (Ajayan and Balasubramanian 2020). When fiscal cutbacks occur, the pressure to maintain research performance becomes even more acute; institutions are forced to sustain or accelerate output levels even when financial incentives and direct support is declines (Bak and Kim 2023). At the core of this management system is the corporate premise that academic institutions are structurally no different from any commercial enterprise and can therefore be optimised through auditing and performance-monitoring systems (Hasham 2018). Consequently, the historical evolution of research performance measurement systems, particularly within heavily evaluated sectors like Australian higher education, outlines a steady intensification of administrative oversight (Martin-Sardesai et al. 2019).

title: Describing the SMU-affiliated Research Corpus
section: Institutional Leadership and Strategic Shared Visions
text:
Institutional Leadership and Strategic Shared Visions
A central tenet of corporate strategic planning is that institutional leadership is in a position to steer research excellence. Recent quantitative modeling of presidential capabilities in Chinese higher education argues that specific strategic competencies at the executive level correlate positively with institutional performance gains and international visibility (Dong, Wu, and Yu 2025). Similarly, evaluations of academic leadership and university performance across European and Russian contexts investigate whether universities demonstrate measurable improvements when led by active, highly cited scholars who embody research excellence, rather than pure career administrators (Gerashchenko 2022). This structural steering is frequently reinforced by regional contagion effects, where the strategic choices and performance trajectories of neighbouring peer institutions create a normative pressure that drives local academic leadership to adopt identical strategic management models (Saftiuc, Proscanu, and Teodorescu 2025).
For these administrative plans to translate into scholarly output, university leaders direct attention to building an institutional shared vision that attempts to bridge the historical divide between research and teaching mandates (Bui et al. 2024). Senior management relies on transformational leadership styles, operating under the assumption that inspiring a collective corporate identity will foster internal creativity and outputs (Salim and Zakaria 2021). In fields such as green innovation and technology transfer, evidence indicates that the specific academic and corporate experiences of the top management team can shape the volume and direction of institutional innovation outputs (Zhao et al. 2021). Moreover, when academic executives retain active boardroom connections, they can connect lab-based research with high-impact industrial commercialisation, demonstrating how top-down strategies attempt to steer basic science toward applied economic utility (Zhu, Wu, and Gaidai 2025).

title: Describing the SMU-affiliated Research Corpus
text:
Guiding Research Productivity
At the level of the faculty member, the primary mechanisms used to enforce strategic alignment are institutional incentives, formal performance appraisals, and individual research productivity tracking. Evidence suggests that while structured interventions can alter short-term output counts, they rarely change long-term scholarly trajectories (Ryazanova and Jaskiene 2022). While routine bibliometric reports are frequently positioned as one tool among many, these data summaries often function as coercive monitoring mechanisms that hold individual faculty accountable to generic performance targets (Cabezas-Clavijo and Torres-Salinas 2021). In some cases, advanced institutional frameworks have emerged, such as bibliometric strength, potential, and risk analysis models, which allow administrators to track exactly how faculty publication choices respond to central strategic choices and funding pathways (Iping et al. 2024).
The efficacy of these incentive structures remains dependent on localized professional contexts and personal scholarly investments. In Canada, broad empirical studies of primary care researchers demonstrate that productivity is strongly associated with protected research time, dedicated infrastructure, and targeted team-based funding rather than purely top-down corporate mandates (Aggarwal et al. 2024). Furthermore, the specialized nature of research production is heavily reliant on specific cognitive resources and long-term personal investments, which means that arbitrary administrative redirections can result in cognitive friction and operational inefficiency for the scholar (Degli Antoni, Fia, and Sacconi 2022). Quantitative analyses of individual academic research agendas confirm that broader organizational factors and institutional priorities interact directly with disciplinary traditions, meaning that top-down steering tools must constantly compete with an academic’s internalized scholarly values and peer networks (Horta and Santos 2020).

title: Describing the SMU-affiliated Research Corpus
text:
Tensions, Resistance, and Academic Freedom
The imposition of corporate performance management has generated tensions, with many scholars arguing that these frameworks stifle academic freedom and distort genuine knowledge production. Critical discourse analyses highlight that aggressive performance management frameworks force a precarious state of affairs upon academic work, transforming scholarly writing into a rushed commodity designed to satisfy auditing cycles rather than solve profound intellectual problems (Morrish and Sauntson 2016). This shift creates a sense of alienation, where academic identities are systematically reconfigured to fit the parameters of the managed university, sparking widespread subtle resistance among faculty who seek to protect their professional autonomy from neoliberal encroachment (Morrish 2017). In specialized fields like social work education, the imposition of a marketized, neo-liberal agenda is shown to directly compromise the critical, social-justice mission of the discipline by prioritizing commercial metric capture over community engagement (MacDonald and Nixon 2016).
The human cost of these auditing regimes is captured in qualitative terms by academics who describe the modern pressure cooker environment (Xu and Poole 2024). This creates institutional struggles for recognition where individual departments are pitted against one another for scarce resources, fragmenting the university’s traditional community of scholars (Muench and Baier 2012). Moreover, the formal policies and administrative structures often lack meaningful faculty buy-in because they are perceived as top-down compliance exercises rather than authentic scholarly transformations (Castro-Gomez et al. 2026). Without aligning internal policy incentives directly with the intrinsic motivations and professional values of the faculty, centralized administrative mandates fail to cultivate genuine participation or sustainable scholarly growth (Barsallo et al. 2026).

title: Describing the SMU-affiliated Research Corpus
text:
Do Strategic Research Plans Work?
This breief review on higher education management demonstrates a conflict between top-down corporate steering and bottom-up faculty behaviour. While institutional theories and administrative models posit that clear leadership capabilities, shared corporate visions, and targeted bibliometric monitoring can successfully optimize and direct an institution’s research performance, empirical accounts expose resistance, strategic gaming, and profound alignment failures. This contradiction exposes a gap in evaluative scientometrics: we lack robust, objective, longitudinal measures of whether corporate university strategies genuinely shape the intellectual landscape of an institution or if they merely retroactively rebrand pre-existing, faculty-driven strengths.
It is with this in mind that I raise the following question: do strategic research plans work?
I explore this question turning to the research corpus of Saint Mary’s University (SMU).

title: Describing the SMU-affiliated Research Corpus
text:
Data
This bibliometric study examines 36 years of SMU-affiliated research, from January 1990 through December 2025. The corpus is restricted to publications for which the institutional affiliation metadata explicitly identifies SMU. No restrictions were placed on document type. These deliberately broad parameters were intended to capture the full range of scholarly outputs indexed by Web of Science (WoS) that can be attributed to faculty, staff, and researchers associated with SMU, providing a basis for examining publication behaviour, research activity, and patterns of connection and collaboration across the university community over the period.
The search produced a corpus of 7,850 publications appearing across 2,862 different publication sources, reflecting a wide range of scholarly venues and the disciplinary breadth of the university. The corpus should not, however, be treated as a complete inventory of everything produced at SMU. Web of Science is widely used for bibliometric research, but, like all bibliographic databases, it is selective. Its coverage tends to favour English-language journals and disciplines in which journal articles and collaborative publication are dominant forms of scholarly communication. Fields in which research is more often communicated through books, book chapters, regional journals, professional publications, or other locally oriented venues may therefore be less completely represented. This is particularly consequential for some areas of the humanities and social sciences. The analysis should accordingly be understood as a description of the SMU research activity visible through Web of Science rather than an exhaustive account of the university’s entire research culture.

title: Keyword Co-occurance Analysis
text:
I use keyword co-occurrence analysis to examine the substantive organization of the SMU-affiliated corpus. The method belongs to the same broad family of bibliometric techniques as co-citation and co-author analysis, but its object is different: rather than asking which authors collaborate or which publications are cited together, it asks which research keywords co-occur across a collection of publications. Authors and databases use keywords to characterize the content of a publication, typically identifying concepts, topics, methods, populations, objects of study, or research problems. The underlying assumption is that these keywords are not distributed randomly. When two keywords repeatedly appear together in the same publications, that recurrence provides evidence that the ideas are being brought into relation within the literature. Co-word analysis therefore allows me to move from a collection of individual publications to a representation of the substantive relationships that recur across the corpus, without beginning from a predetermined classification of the literature.
A keyword co-occurrence network is constructed by first counting these relationships. In the simplified example, a co-occurrence matrix contains six research keywords in its rows and columns, with each intersecting cell recording how many times a pair of keywords appears together. Sport and Identity, for example, have a co-occurrence value of five, whereas Identity and Network Analysis co-occur only once.

The matrix is then converted into an undirected, weighted network using methods of network analysis. Each keyword becomes a node, and an edge connects two nodes when the corresponding keywords occur together in at least one publication. The weight of the edge records the frequency of that co-occurrence, allowing more recurrent relationships to be represented by thicker lines.
Once represented as a network, additional measures can be used to describe the position of individual keywords and the structure of the network as a whole. Degree records the number of other keywords to which a keyword is directly connected, so a high-degree keyword is more extensively embedded in the network than one with relatively few connections. Clustering algorithms such as Louvain identify groups of keywords that are more densely connected to one another than to the rest of the network.
Example Keyword Co-Occurrence Network
In the toy example, Masculinity, Sport, and Identity form one such group, while Network Analysis, Bibliometrics, and Data Science form another. The strongest relationships include Network Analysis–Bibliometrics (6), Sport–Identity (5), and Bibliometrics–Data Science (5). By contrast, the single co-occurrence between Identity and Network Analysis creates a comparatively weak bridge between the two clusters. The visualization therefore makes both internal cohesion and cross-cluster connection visible. Spatial position should be interpreted cautiously, however, because it is partly a consequence of the layout algorithm rather than an independent substantive property.
What the resulting network reveals is not simply which keywords are common, but how the substantive vocabulary of a research corpus is organized relationally. Nodes identify the concepts present in the literature; degree indicates how broadly those concepts are connected; edge weights show which associations recur more or less frequently; and clusters identify concentrations of keywords that repeatedly occur together. When the highly connected keywords within a cluster point toward a coherent substantive concern, those clusters can reasonably be interpreted as research areas or thematic formations. The network can also identify bridging concepts that connect otherwise distinct areas of research and more peripheral keywords that occupy specialized positions.

title: Keyword Co-occurance Analysis
text:
The SMU-affiliated keyword network
In what follows, I use keyword co-occurrence analysis to map recurring intellectual associations within the SMU-affiliated corpus of 7,850 publications. The network focuses on how the keywords used to describe those publications are connected. Groups of densely connected keywords are represented as clusters, but these clusters should not be understood as predetermined departments, disciplines, or administrative categories. They are emergent groupings of concepts, research problems, methods, populations, and objects of study that recur together across the corpus. The resulting network therefore provides a way of examining both what SMU-affiliated researchers study and how different areas of research are related within the indexed literature.
A connection between two keywords indicates that the keywords have been used together in describing the same scholarly output; it does not imply that they have the same meaning or necessarily belong to the same discipline. What matters analytically is the pattern of relationships among keywords. A keyword may be highly connected because it appears alongside many different topics, while another may occupy a more specialized position because its connections are concentrated within a narrower area of research. The network is therefore best understood as a map of research association and connectedness rather than simply a count of topics.
The network combines two forms of keyword metadata. Author keywords are keywords selected by authors to describe the subject matter of their publications, while database-generated keywords, such as Keywords Plus, are derived from information in the bibliographic record to identify additional topical relationships. These were combined before constructing the network to provide a broader representation of the subjects and concepts associated with each publication. As a result, a node labelled migration, galaxies, or education represents a keyword in the bibliographic description of the corpus, not a researcher, department, publication, or project.
The vocabulary itself is heterogeneous. Some keywords identify broad substantive areas, while others refer to theoretical concepts, research methods, populations, geographic locations, objects of study, scientific processes, or highly specialized phenomena. Because author-supplied and database-generated keywords are combined, the network should be interpreted as a representation of how SMU research is bibliographically described and connected, rather than as a direct inventory of the concepts researchers themselves would necessarily identify as most important.

title: Keyword Co-occurance Analysis
section: How to use the network and tables
text:
How to use the network and tables
The interactive network provides the broadest view of these relationships. Use the keyword search above the network to locate a particular keyword. Selecting a keyword highlights its node in yellow with a black border. Once selected, the nodes connected directly to that keyword are also highlighted. The network can then be zoomed and panned to bring these linked nodes into focus, and individual nodes may be dragged to make crowded areas easier to inspect. Moving a node changes only its position on the screen and does not alter the underlying network analysis.
When you look at a keyword together with all of its neighbours, you are looking at that keyword’s immediate local network. The selected keyword is the focal keyword, and each neighbour is another keyword that appeared with it in the metadata of at least one publication in the corpus. The neighbourhood therefore shows the set of topics, concepts, methods, populations, places, or objects of study that have been directly associated with that keyword in SMU-affiliated research. This neighbourhood can be interpreted as a picture of the keyword’s intellectual context. A keyword with neighbours drawn largely from its own cluster is embedded mainly within a relatively concentrated area of research. Selecting the keywords “behaviour”, “radial velocities”, “health”, “management history”, or “actor network theory” from the keyword drop down search menu offers an illustration of this type of pattern. A keyword whose neighbours span several clusters may instead connect otherwise distinct areas of scholarly activity. Selecting the keywords “origin”, “sequence”, or “evolution” will illustrate this type of pattern.
Nodes with the same colour belong to the same intellectual cluster.1 Node size represents degree of connectedness: larger nodes are directly connected to a greater number of other keywords in the network, while smaller nodes have fewer direct connections and tend to occupy more specialized positions. Node size therefore represents network connectedness rather than the quality, importance, or volume of research associated with a keyword.
The tables provide complementary ways of examining the same network.

The Keyword neighbours table allows a reader to select an exact keyword and retrieve all of the keywords directly connected to it, ordered by the strength of their co-occurrence. This value is a measure of how often the focal keyword and a particular neighbour appear together in the publication metadata. For example, searching for the keyword “health” in this table reveals that “health” and “canada” co-occur 9 times in this dataset.
The Cluster profiles table provides a compact overview of the vocabulary associated with each intellectual cluster.
The Cluster vocabulary table lists every keyword in the network by cluster, allowing readers to move beyond the most prominent keywords and examine more specialized areas that may be difficult to identify visually.
The Author lookup table will return the titles of publications of an author. This presented partly as a means of allowing those interested to think through and assess the coverage of the WoS database.

The Cluster profiles and Cluster vocabulary look up tables provide insight into the structure of these clusters. The tables report each keyword’s rank and degree.2

section: If you’ve made it this far…
text:
If you’ve made it this far…
On this basis of the above, what begins to emerge is that the SMU-affiliated research corpus contains 8 research clusters whose “identities” have yet to be specified.
In the same way that the all the keywords used in the SMU-affiliated corpus can be arranged in a network and “decomposed” into 8 clusters, each of these 8 clusters can be explored in the same way. “Decomposing” these research clusters allows for their structure to be explored more carefully, opening up an opportunity to think more clearly about what each of these 8 research clusters is “about”–and what this might say about the university as a whole.
To that end, eventually, at the top of the page, you’ll find links to details about each of the 8 research clusters. Currently, only data for Research Cluster Two is available. In the spirit of “member checking” (Birt et al. 2016; McKim 2023), I invite you to review these details. Does this data resonate with your understanding of your own scholarly activity and/or the activity at SMU?
